statement: A register of the internal and external issues that affect the organization's security outcomes is kept, including climate change where it is relevant. The register is reviewed on a defined cycle and when the business context changes. Each review is recorded so the program stays tied to real conditions.
why_asked: Without a view of the issues around it, the program is built for yesterday's risks and drifts away from the business.
how_to_ask: Ask how the organization learns what is changing in its market, technology, regulation and physical environment, and who records it. Ask whether climate change was considered and what was decided. Example probe: "Show me where you wrote down the issues that shape your security priorities, and when you last updated them."
question: Does your organization keep current the internal or external issues, including climate change where relevant, that affect its security outcomes?
expected_evidence: Register or analysis of internal and external issues; record of the climate change relevance decision; review minutes or version history showing updates over the last two review cycles
good_looks_like: A dated register lists internal and external issues with an owner. It records a clear yes or no on climate change with the reason. It shows updates after major changes and feeds scope, risk and objective setting.
test: Obtain the issues register. Check it covers both internal and external issues and records the climate change decision. Pass if the register is current, owned, and shows at least one review in the last two cycles.
baseline_risk: The security program ignores shifts in the business or environment and protects against the wrong things.

statement: A register is kept of the parties with a stake in security, such as customers, regulators, partners and staff. For each party the register states the requirements, including any climate-related ones, and whether the security program will address them. It is reviewed on a defined cycle and when a party or its requirements change.
why_asked: If stakeholder expectations are not captured, the program can miss contractual or regulatory duties and be surprised by them.
how_to_ask: Ask who the organization considers its interested parties and how it learns what they expect. Look for a recorded decision on which requirements are taken on. Example probe: "Which customers or regulators have security requirements for you, and where are those written down with a decision on each?"
question: Does your organization maintain a register of the parties with a stake in its security, with their requirements?
expected_evidence: Interested parties register; record of requirements per party; record of decisions on which requirements are addressed; review history for the last two cycles
good_looks_like: The register names each party, lists its requirements in plain terms, and marks each requirement as addressed or not, with the reason. It is reviewed on a set cycle and feeds scope and the legal register.
test: Obtain the interested parties register. Take five parties and check each has stated requirements and a recorded decision. Pass if all sampled parties are complete and the register was reviewed in the last two cycles.
baseline_risk: Stakeholder requirements go unmet, leading to lost contracts, regulatory findings or surprise demands.

statement: The scope of the security program is defined and documented, covering its boundaries and where it applies. The scope takes account of the organization's issues, stakeholder requirements and dependencies on other parties. It is approved and reviewed when the business changes.
why_asked: An unclear scope leaves critical systems, sites or services unprotected, or makes any assurance claim misleading.
how_to_ask: Ask for the scope statement and how it was decided. Check what is in and out, and why. Example probe: "Which sites, systems and services are inside your security program, and who approved leaving anything out?"
question: Does your organization document the scope of its security program?
expected_evidence: Scope statement with boundaries and exclusions; approval record; version history; record of dependencies on other parties
good_looks_like: The scope statement names the locations, business units, services and systems covered. Each exclusion has a reason. It cites the issues, stakeholder requirements and dependencies considered and carries management approval.
test: Obtain the scope statement. Compare it to the asset inventory and a list of business units. Pass if it is approved, current, and every sampled unit or system is either inside scope or has a recorded exclusion reason.
baseline_risk: Unprotected assets sit outside the program, and assurance statements overstate what is covered.

statement: A security management system is established, run and maintained, with defined processes and the way they interact. Each process has an assigned owner, and a check on a defined cycle confirms the system is running and being improved. Proof is a process map, owner list and review records.
why_asked: Without a working management system, security is a set of one-off activities that fade when people change.
how_to_ask: Ask how the organization's security processes fit together and who owns each. Look for evidence the system is used, not only written. Example probe: "Walk me through how risk, incidents and audits feed each other, and show me a recent example."
question: Does your organization operate a security management system with defined processes?
expected_evidence: Security management system description or process map; process owner list; examples of processes in operation; improvement records from the current review period
good_looks_like: A process map shows each security process, its owner and its inputs and outputs. Records show the processes running and feeding improvements, with changes tracked.
test: Obtain the process map and owner list. Pick three processes and trace one recent run of each through to records. Pass if each has a named owner and a dated record of operation in the last cycle.
baseline_risk: Security work stays ad hoc, so gaps recur and results depend on individuals.

statement: Top management leads the security program. It sets policy and objectives that fit the strategy, builds security needs into business processes, and makes sure the program achieves its intended outcomes. It communicates why security matters, directs and supports the people who run the program, supports other managers in leading in their own areas, and promotes improvement. Sign-offs and minutes are the proof.
why_asked: Programs without visible leadership lose budget and priority, and staff treat security as optional.
how_to_ask: Ask senior leaders how they set direction, where security shows up in business planning and how they back those who run the security program. Example probe: "Tell me about the last time a business decision changed because of a security concern. Where is that recorded?"
question: Does your top management actively lead the security program?
expected_evidence: Management meeting minutes with security items; approved policy and objectives; examples of security built into business processes; leadership communications on security; records from the current review period
good_looks_like: Leaders approve policy and objectives that cite the strategy. Security appears in project, procurement and planning processes. Minutes and messages show leaders directing and supporting the program.
test: Review leadership minutes and communications for the period. Sample three business processes for built-in security steps and check that the program's outcomes are reviewed. Pass if leadership actions are recorded, the sampled processes include security steps, outcomes are reviewed, and policy and objectives show approval.
baseline_risk: Security lacks authority and resources, and the program fails when it meets business resistance.

statement: A set of security policies headed by a top-level policy is maintained, with each policy approved by management. The policies are published, acknowledged by personnel and relevant outside parties, and reviewed on a defined cycle and after significant change. Proof is the approval record, distribution list, acknowledgements and review log.
why_asked: Policies set the rules everything else relies on. If they are missing, unapproved or stale, staff have no clear standard to follow.
how_to_ask: Ask for the policy list and sample how each was approved, shared and reviewed. Check that outsiders such as suppliers receive the relevant ones. Example probe: "Show me your top-level policy, who approved it, and how a new joiner acknowledges it."
question: Does your organization maintain a management-approved set of security policies that it reviews on a defined cycle?
expected_evidence: Top-level security policy; topic policies such as access control, backup and cryptography; approval records; distribution list; acknowledgement records; version history or review log for the last review cycle
good_looks_like: A top-level policy and topic policies exist, each with management approval and an owner. They are published, staff and relevant outsiders acknowledge them, and each has a recorded review within its interval or after major change.
test: Obtain the policy list. Sample five policies including the top-level one. Check approval, publication, acknowledgement records and last review date. Pass if all sampled policies are approved and in date, and acknowledgements exist for staff.
baseline_risk: Staff and partners act without clear rules, and the organization cannot show management intent.

statement: Security roles, responsibilities and authorities are defined and each is assigned to a named, current person. This includes responsibility for program conformity and for reporting performance to top management. The assignments are communicated and rechecked when people or structures change, using a role document or RACI with names.
why_asked: If roles are unnamed or out of date, tasks fall between people and no one answers for security results.
how_to_ask: Ask for the role document and check names against the current staff list. Ask who reports program performance upward. Example probe: "Who is responsible for reporting security performance to the board, and where is that written?"
question: Does your organization assign each security role to a named person?
expected_evidence: Roles and responsibilities document or RACI with names; security organization chart; communication record of assignments; update history for the last review cycle
good_looks_like: Each security role has a written responsibility set and a named, current holder. Conformity and reporting duties are assigned. Changes in staff trigger an update.
test: Obtain the RACI and a current staff list. Sample five roles and confirm each holder is current. Pass if every sampled role is defined, assigned to a named current person, and conformity and reporting duties are assigned.
baseline_risk: Duties are missed or disputed, and incidents and audits find no accountable owner.

statement: Every team member is required to work in line with the organization's security policies and procedures. The requirement is stated in documents each person receives, such as a code of conduct or onboarding pack. Teams are briefed or acknowledgements are tracked, and the records are kept.
why_asked: Rules that are not reinforced inside teams are routinely ignored, and nobody is clearly responsible for lapses.
how_to_ask: Ask how team members learn that following security policy is expected and how that is reinforced in each team. Look for records, not statements. Example probe: "Show me the last briefing on security expectations in one team and how you know everyone was reached."
question: Does your organization make sure every team member knows they must work in line with its security policies and procedures?
expected_evidence: Code of conduct, onboarding pack or briefing guide stating the expectation; policy acknowledgement tracking; team briefing records; records from the current review period
good_looks_like: A document each team member receives states that following security policy is required. Briefings or tracked acknowledgements cover every team, with records for the period.
test: Obtain the document stating the expectation and the acknowledgement or briefing records. Sample three teams. Pass if the expectation is documented and each sampled team has a briefing or acknowledgement record in the period.
baseline_risk: Security is treated as someone else's job, and non-compliance goes unchallenged.

statement: A record is kept of the specialist security forums and professional groups the organization joins or follows. Participation is active, and relevant advisories and lessons are circulated to those who need them. Proof is a membership list and circulation records.
why_asked: Teams that stay isolated miss emerging threats, advisories and good practice that peers already use.
how_to_ask: Ask which groups, mailing lists or industry bodies the organization follows and what has come out of them recently. Example probe: "What was the last advisory from a security group that changed something you did?"
question: Does your organization keep contact with specialist security forums or professional groups?
expected_evidence: List of forums, groups or subscriptions; advisories received and circulated; event attendance records; records from the current review period
good_looks_like: A list names each group with an internal contact. Advisories and lessons are circulated, and at least one example shows learning being acted on.
test: Obtain the membership or subscription list and circulation records. Sample three recent advisories. Pass if the list is current and each sampled item shows it was received and passed on to a responsible person.
baseline_risk: The organization learns of new threats and practices late, from its own incidents.

statement: The risks and opportunities that bear on the security program are determined, actions for them are planned, and those actions are built into program processes. A method for checking that the actions work is planned as well. Proof is a planning record with owners and a method for evaluating results.
why_asked: Skipping this planning step means the program reacts to problems and misses chances to improve.
how_to_ask: Ask how the organization decides what could stop the program working and what could help it, and how actions are tracked. Detailed risk assessment is covered elsewhere. Example probe: "Show me the program-level risks and opportunities you recorded and the action taken on one."
question: Does your organization plan actions for the risks and opportunities that bear on its security program?
expected_evidence: Program-level risk and opportunity register or planning record; action plan with owners; evidence of effectiveness checks; review records for the last cycle
good_looks_like: Program risks and opportunities are listed with owners and planned actions. Actions are built into the processes, and each states how its effect will be checked, with results recorded.
test: Obtain the planning record. Sample three actions and trace each to a process change and an effectiveness check. Pass if all sampled actions have an owner, a built-in step and a recorded check.
baseline_risk: The program fails to anticipate obstacles and overlooks chances to improve.

statement: Measurable security objectives are set at relevant functions, consistent with policy. For each objective the plan states what will be done, with what resources, by whom, by when and how results are evaluated. Objectives are monitored, communicated and updated, and the plan is kept as a record.
why_asked: Vague aims cannot be tracked, so the program cannot show whether it is succeeding.
how_to_ask: Ask for the current objectives and how each is measured. Look for owners, dates and results. Example probe: "Which security objective did you miss last period, and what did you change?"
question: Does your organization set measurable security objectives with a plan to meet them?
expected_evidence: Security objectives with measures; objective plans showing actions, resources, owners and dates; progress reports; communication records for the last cycle
good_looks_like: Each objective is measurable, linked to policy and risk results, and has an owner, resources and due date. Progress is reported, objectives are updated as needed and staff know them.
test: Obtain the objectives and plans. Sample three objectives and check each is measurable and has resources, owner, date and a progress record. Pass if all sampled objectives meet these tests.
baseline_risk: The program has no way to show progress, and effort drifts toward low-value work.

statement: Any needed change to the security management system is carried out in a planned way. Each change is recorded with its purpose, effects, resources and owner, and is approved before it is made. Proof is a change record or plan.
why_asked: Unplanned changes to the program can break processes and leave gaps no one notices.
how_to_ask: Ask for a recent change to the program, such as a new process or scope shift, and how it was planned and approved. Example probe: "Walk me through the last change you made to how the program works."
question: Does your organization carry out needed changes to its security management system in a planned way?
expected_evidence: Change records or plans for program changes; approval records; impact notes; records from the current review period
good_looks_like: Changes are proposed with a reason, impact and owner and are approved before being made. Records show the change was completed and communicated.
test: Obtain the list of changes to the program in the period. Sample three and check for purpose, impact review, approval and completion. Pass if all sampled changes have these records.
baseline_risk: Ad hoc changes introduce gaps or contradictions into the program.

statement: The resources needed to establish, run, maintain and improve the security program are determined and provided, including people, budget and tools. Resource needs are assessed on a defined cycle and when scope or risk changes. Proof is an approved budget and staffing plan.
why_asked: An under-resourced program cannot deliver its commitments, whatever the policies say.
how_to_ask: Ask how the security budget and staffing are decided and who confirms they are enough. Example probe: "When did you last ask for more resources, what was decided, and what was the effect?"
question: Does your organization provide the resources its security program needs?
expected_evidence: Approved security budget; staffing plan or headcount record; resource request and decision records; records from the current review period
good_looks_like: Resource needs are linked to objectives and risks, approved by top management and tracked. Gaps are reported, and decisions on requests are recorded.
test: Obtain the budget, staffing plan and resource requests. Check approvals against objectives. Pass if resources are approved, requests were decided and recorded, and any gap has a documented decision.
baseline_risk: The program cannot meet its objectives, and known work goes undone for lack of people or tools.

statement: What security matters need communicating is decided, along with when, to whom and how, both inside and outside the organization. This is kept as a communication plan and checked on a defined cycle. Proof is the plan and examples of messages sent.
why_asked: Without a plan, the right people do not hear about security matters at the right time.
how_to_ask: Ask who gets told what about security, and how outside parties such as regulators and customers are reached. Example probe: "Show me your communication plan and the last message sent under it."
question: Does your organization have a plan for communicating about security internally or externally?
expected_evidence: Security communication plan or matrix; examples of internal and external communications; review records for the last cycle
good_looks_like: A plan lists topics, audiences, timing, senders and channels for internal and external communication. Examples show it is followed and reviewed.
test: Obtain the communication plan. Sample three entries and find a sent example for each. Pass if all sampled entries show the planned audience and channel was used at the planned time.
baseline_risk: Important security information is missed or sent to the wrong people, delaying action.

statement: The documented information the security program needs is kept, and how it is created, approved, updated, distributed, protected, retained and disposed of is controlled. Each document has an identifier, owner, version and review date. Documents of outside origin that the program needs are identified and controlled in the same way.
why_asked: Uncontrolled documents lead to staff using outdated rules and lost or leaked records.
how_to_ask: Ask how documents are numbered, approved and stored, and how old versions are handled. Example probe: "Pick one procedure and show me its version history and who approved the current one."
question: Does your organization control the documented information its security program needs, from creation through disposal?
expected_evidence: Document control procedure; document register with versions and owners; approval records; access and retention settings; examples of outside documents that are controlled
good_looks_like: A document register lists identifier, owner, version, approval and review date. Access and retention rules are applied, old versions are removed from use, and outside documents are tracked.
test: Obtain the document register. Sample five documents and check identification, approval, version, access and retention. Pass if all sampled documents meet these tests.
baseline_risk: Staff rely on outdated or unapproved documents, and sensitive records are exposed or lost.

statement: The processes needed to meet security requirements and carry out treatment actions are planned, run and controlled, with set criteria for those processes. Planned changes are controlled, the effect of unplanned ones is reviewed, and externally provided processes, products and services are controlled. Records show processes ran as planned.
why_asked: Plans mean little if day-to-day operation is not controlled, especially where work is outsourced or changes slip through.
how_to_ask: Ask how operational security processes are defined and checked, how changes are controlled and how outsourced work is kept in line. Example probe: "Show me an unplanned change and what you did to review its effect."
question: Does your organization control the day-to-day processes that deliver its security requirements?
expected_evidence: Operational process records showing runs as planned; change records including unplanned changes and reviews; list of outsourced processes and oversight records; records from the current review period
good_looks_like: Processes have defined criteria and records showing they ran as planned. Planned changes are controlled, unplanned changes are reviewed for effect, and each outsourced process has an owner and oversight.
test: Sample three operational processes, one change including an unplanned change, and one externally provided process, product or service. Check the criteria and records of operation, review and oversight. Pass if each sample shows a controlled, recorded result.
baseline_risk: Controls exist on paper but processes drift, and outsourced work runs without oversight.

statement: What security performance to measure is decided, with methods that give valid, comparable and reproducible results, and when and by whom it is measured. When and by whom results are analyzed is also set. Results and the effectiveness of the program are evaluated on a defined cycle, and evidence is kept. Proof is a metrics list, reports and review notes.
why_asked: Without measurement, the organization cannot tell whether its security is working or getting worse.
how_to_ask: Ask which measures the organization tracks and what decisions have come from them. Example probe: "Which security metric moved last quarter, and what did you do about it?"
question: Does your organization measure and evaluate its security performance?
expected_evidence: Metrics definitions with methods and owners; performance reports; evaluation notes or dashboards; records from the current review period
good_looks_like: Each metric has a definition, method, owner and cycle. Reports are produced on schedule, assessed against targets and used to drive action.
test: Obtain the metrics list and reports for the period. Sample three metrics and check definition, method, collection, analysis and evaluation records, including who and when. Pass if every sampled metric has all of them and was reported on its cycle.
baseline_risk: Problems stay hidden until an incident, and leaders have no basis for decisions.

statement: Top management reviews the security program at planned intervals. The review covers the status of past actions, changes in issues and in the needs of interested parties, performance trends (nonconformities, measurements, audit results and objectives), feedback from interested parties, risk results and treatment status, and improvement opportunities. Decisions on improvement and needed changes are recorded and tracked.
why_asked: A review that skips inputs or leaves no decisions fails to steer the program or correct it.
how_to_ask: Ask for the last management review pack and minutes. Check the inputs covered and the decisions taken. Example probe: "Show me the decisions from your last management review and where each stands."
question: Does your top management review the security program at planned intervals?
expected_evidence: Management review agenda and inputs pack; signed minutes with decisions; action tracker; reviews from the last two cycles
good_looks_like: The review happens on schedule with top management present. All defined inputs are covered, decisions on improvement and changes are recorded with owners, and earlier actions are followed up.
test: Obtain minutes of the last two reviews. Check each covers all defined inputs and has recorded decisions. Pass if both reviews occurred on plan with all inputs and each decision has an owner.
baseline_risk: Leaders lose sight of program health, and known problems are never decided on.

statement: The suitability, adequacy and effectiveness of the security program are continually improved. Improvement opportunities come from reviews, audits, incidents and measures. They are logged, prioritized, owned and tracked to completion.
why_asked: Programs that do not improve fall behind changing threats and business needs.
how_to_ask: Ask for the improvement log and examples of improvements made. Look for source, owner and outcome. Example probe: "Name two improvements made this year and what triggered them."
question: Does your organization continually improve its security program?
expected_evidence: Improvement log or register; completed improvement records; links to reviews, audits or incidents that triggered them; records from the current review period
good_looks_like: An improvement log records each idea with source, owner, priority and status. Completed items show the benefit, and trends show the program getting better.
test: Obtain the improvement log. Sample three completed items and check source, owner and outcome. Pass if each sampled item is traceable from source to completion with a recorded result.
baseline_risk: The program stagnates, and the same weaknesses recur year after year.

statement: Each nonconformity is controlled and corrected, and its consequences are dealt with. Whether to remove the cause is evaluated, action is taken, and a review confirms the action worked and changes the program if needed. All nonconformities and actions are recorded in a log.
why_asked: Fixing symptoms without causes lets the same failures return, and untracked findings are forgotten.
how_to_ask: Ask for the corrective action log and pick items from audits and incidents. Check root cause and effectiveness checks. Example probe: "Show me a finding from an audit and the evidence its fix worked."
question: Does your organization correct nonconformities and remove their causes?
expected_evidence: Nonconformity and corrective action log; root cause analyses; effectiveness check records; closure approvals; records from the current review period
good_looks_like: Each nonconformity is logged with the correction, cause analysis, action, owner and due date. Closure needs a check that the fix worked, and overdue items are escalated.
test: Obtain the corrective action log for the period. Sample five closed items and check correction, root cause, action and effectiveness review. Pass if all sampled items are complete with a recorded effectiveness check.
baseline_risk: Findings recur and audit issues stay open with no accountable fix.
